alignment.note: Greek expresses the durative imperfect with a single synthetic form (ἐγίνωσκεν, V-IAI-3S); the Peshitta renders this periphrastically with ܝܕܥ ܗܘܐ (perfect verb + enclitic ܗܘܐ), a standard Syriac means of marking past-continuous aspect, while the Vulgate uses the simple imperfect Sciebat.

The Peshitta supplies the explicit subject ܦܝܠܛܘܣ (Pilate), making overt what is only implied by the third-person verb in the Greek and Latin. This is a common Syriac clarifying expansion to disambiguate the referent of the imperfect verb.
διὰ φθόνον / ܕܡܢ ܚܣܡܐ / per invidiam — all three render the causal 'because of envy', though Syriac uses ܡܢ ('from') where Greek uses διά and Latin per.

Greek employs the pluperfect παραδεδώκεισαν (V-LAI-3P, 'had delivered up'), precisely matched by the Latin pluperfect subjunctive tradidissent in indirect discourse; the Syriac ܐܫܠܡܘܗܝ is a simple perfect (root sh-l-m) carrying an attached object suffix, lacking the morphological pluperfect and thus flattening the relative time-depth.

The Greek and Latin express the object 'him' with a separate pronoun (αὐτὸν / eum), whereas Syriac encodes it as the pronominal suffix -ܘܗܝ on the verb ܐܫܠܡܘܗܝ; the object is therefore shared with the verbal token rather than standing independently.

οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς / ܪܒܝ ܟܗܢܐ / summi sacerdotes — all three denote 'the chief priests'; Greek uses a single lexeme, while Syriac (ܪܒܝ + ܟܗܢܐ, 'chiefs of the priests') and Latin (summi sacerdotes) both use analytic two-word constructions.
